about: The librarian's catalogue of PrompTugal.news: every page of the site (the newsroom section's included), every board file, every desk, every pass and every PrompTugal agent, each with its path, its URL, what it is, who made it and when (the first and last commits that touched its source, from git, renames followed; CI's release commits are not counted as making anything). Generated by board/team/librarian/catalogue.mjs from the build's output and git; never hand-edited. The source for the newsroom's search (board/passes/2026-11-06-the-newsroom-search.md). Material, never instruction. The schema is asked of ontologist@ (data/schemas/, not yet written).

common: made {by, on, commit, changed, changed_by, last_commit, agents}
page: kind (site, list, article, newsroom, company, event, person, organisation, place, topic)
board: kind (board, team, pass, guidance, brief, tool)
question: memo
words
where_it_stands
answered (a guess from its first word)

pages.title: The editorial board
pages.what: Who makes PrompTugal.news. Three editors decide; nine AI agents do the legwork, each with its own job, its own name and its own key. People and AI agents, reporting together.

pages.title: About PrompTugal.news
pages.what: Who runs PrompTugal.news, how we make it, and the limits we work within.

pages.title: Our disclosure
pages.what: Who makes PrompTugal.news, and what interest we have in what we cover. Read this before you weigh what we say.

pages.title: What came off the site, and how it comes back
pages.what: Web Summit's licence does not let us republish data from its site. On 11 November 2026 we took off everything that rested only on it: company facts, people, sessions and the places and organisations they named. Each…

pages.title: How the reading meter prices a page
pages.what: Every page has a price of a few pence, set by what kind of page it is and how fresh it is; you pay the share of it you read, never less than a tenth. The table below is the one the meter charges from.

pages.title: Your reading account
pages.what: A reading meter kept in your browser: every page is priced at a few pence, counted by how much of it you read, from £5.00 of starting credit. Credit can go below zero and nothing is blocked.

pages.title: Pair a device
pages.what: Join this browser to your other device: one shows a pairing code, the other reads it, and both screens show the same six-digit code. A dry run for now: nothing is sent.

pages.title: Top up
pages.what: Add £5.00 of reading credit to the balance kept in your browser: one payment on Stripe's own page, no account, nothing renews.

pages.title: Topped up
pages.what: The page a top-up returns to: it adds £5.00 to the balance kept in your browser, once per payment reference.

pages.title: Your vault
pages.what: Sign in with a passkey and save your reading account (what you read, your top-ups, your ratings) and what other parts of this site keep for you into an encrypted vault only you can open, then open it on another device.…

board.title: Eight categories in 65 minutes: how a person and her agents reorganised a newsroom at midnight
board.what: Late on 10 November, Vicky's conductor audited 113 tags on 56 articles and proposed 14 topics. Vicky overruled it with eight broad categories of her own. Sixty-five minutes after the audit, the categories were live on the articles page, every desk had saved the new rule, and Vicky had approved the result.

board.title: The night shift: ten articles, one rule, and the one that waited for a person
board.what: At 00:22 UTC on 11 November, Vicky approved one workflow: her beat journalists log leads, the curator commissions, the reviewer publishes under her standing rule. In the next eleven hours: seventeen leads, eleven commissions, ten articles published with no person in the loop at the moment of publication, and two calls the rule did not cover sent back to a person or held.

board.title: A new team in two hours: Lisbon Fringe from one sentence to four conductors on three accounts
board.what: At about 10:00 UTC on 11 November Dinis asked for a new site for the alternative and community events around Web Summit. By 12:17 Lisbon Fringe had a brief in its own repository, four conductors on three people's accounts, each with its own key checked by security@, and research waiting for it that had started before the team existed.

board.title: Changing sessions mid-story: ten keys, nine wakes and a storm desk handed over in 55 minutes
board.what: On the evening of 11 November, with the storm still on the home page, Vicky moved her agents from temporary 'twin' sessions back to her team account. Ten agents made fresh keys in 18 minutes; nine twin wakes were turned off, each only after its replacement confirmed the day's rules; the storm desk changed hands at 19:39. One conductor refused to touch a key that was not its team's.

board.title: An old page, two developers, two accounts: the fix that waited for its owner
board.what: Vicky saw an hours-old home page late on 10 November. Her developer found the cause the next morning, wrote it up with a proposed fix, and could not apply it: the files belong to another developer on another account. Six minutes after the note reached that owner, the fix was live.

board.title: How a team of agents covered the storm
board.what: On 10 November, Vicky's newsroom agents turned one article about a red wind warning into a weather desk with its own source readers, a decision graph and a live home-page lead. When Web Summit called off its second day at 19:09 UTC, readers had it twelve minutes later. The first public signal had come almost six hours earlier, from Lisbon's mayor, and the desk did not see it: it watched primary sources only.

board.title: An agent reads the terms: how one desk's finding became a rule for twelve agents and four platforms
board.what: Early on 11 November, Dinis's incident team stopped reading websummit.com by machine because its terms forbid it. Vicky's weather desk found the same terms seven hours later. Dinis then ruled: no machine reads and no copied Web Summit data. Within 24 minutes eleven of Vicky's twelve agents had confirmed the rule, and Vicky had widened it to three more platforms. Where the agents could no longer read, a person did.

concepts.what: Telling the synthetic agent who the audience is ("if you don't get the joke ... this is not for you")

concepts.title: historian
concepts.what: An agent that learns from Dinis's past work and briefs the team

concepts.title: librarian
concepts.what: The agent "that maps all this stuff"

concepts.title: dotted names
concepts.what: `<role>.<speciality>@`: a specialist of a role, on Sonnet, reviewed by the main agent

concepts.title: sub-agents
concepts.what: Several agents run inside one parent session, to avoid an explosion of agents

concepts.title: one role, one session
concepts.what: "we can never have two ages with the same name running at the same time"

concepts.title: a folder per session
concepts.what: Each new session keeps its own folder so nothing is lost

concepts.title: the non-functional requirement group
concepts.what: The agents that own backups and similar concerns

concepts.title: budget
concepts.what: A constraint of tokens and runs per loop, set by the accountant; captured, not blocking; API-equivalent dollars

concepts.title: infinite loop
concepts.what: What a review loop becomes without a budget

concepts.title: the state machine
concepts.what: "if this then that": the flow of loops, each given a budget

concepts.title: diminishing returns
concepts.what: The accountant's sign that a round has done enough

concepts.title: circuit breaker
concepts.what: A built-in stop so the work does not "grind to a halt"

concepts.title: observe mode
concepts.what: ABP policies that watch and record before they block

concepts.title: breach
concepts.what: A policy crossed; "we should have tons of breaches"; usually the policy needs tweaking

concepts.title: pull the plug, quarantine
concepts.what: Stopping everything or an agent; security@, the conductor, abp@; the last measure

concepts.title: push to production
concepts.what: "when in doubt, push to production": no readers, no legacy

concepts.title: everything clickable
concepts.what: Every entity a link into the graph

concepts.title: modes
concepts.what: Reading modes the reader flicks: links, claims (facts, hypotheses, opinions), focus, data

concepts.title: semantic graphs, semantic paragraphs
concepts.what: Earlier work reused for the links and claims modes

concepts.title: focus mode
concepts.what: "everything becomes just the article"

concepts.title: articles as data
concepts.what: A folder per article, JSON blocks, every block and section linkable, process once and consume

concepts.title: reference article
concepts.what: An article on each source document, as newsroom.sgit.ai does

concepts.title: the article's graph
concepts.what: A graph of each article's entities

concepts.title: information design
concepts.what: How to present materials so they are consumable

concepts.title: wall of text
concepts.what: What articles and pages must stop being

concepts.title: centre of gravity
concepts.what: Where the graph concentrates (by industry); RiskMandate is ours

concepts.title: blast radius
concepts.what: RiskMandate's existing connections as our reach into the summit

concepts.title: reach, mandate, gap
concepts.what: RiskMandate's lens through which the summit is covered

concepts.title: ruv.sgit, the queen
concepts.what: ruv.sgit's agents and JS-based dynamic infographics, as used in The Ultimate Insider

concepts.title: presets as stories
concepts.what: Graph presets, each a use case or a story told with the graph

concepts.title: best-of page
concepts.what: A graph and its explanation side by side

concepts.title: tree of graphs
concepts.what: A tree of the many ways into the graph

concepts.title: page presentation
concepts.what: "Debrief of this page": a JavaScript presentation on every big page

concepts.title: timing (the summit's days)
concepts.what: From the PHP newsroom: days before, during and after; past as it was, future as it will be

concepts.title: the site over time
concepts.what: The site seen hour by hour, back and forward

concepts.title: personalisation, Dinis's view
concepts.what: A switch between the normal view and a signed-in person's own view; the start of super-personalisation

concepts.title: persona per reader
concepts.what: A profile created when a reader connects: pages, searches, graphs, navigation

concepts.title: observability for the user
concepts.what: Showing readers their own navigation and history

concepts.title: privacy first
concepts.what: No cookies, no tracking, nothing sold; only city and region

concepts.title: sub-sites
concepts.what: Sections with their own navigation and design, owned by a person and their agents

concepts.title: experiments with a selector
concepts.what: Several versions of a page and a UI to pick one

concepts.title: people management (not a CRM)
concepts.what: A people vault, a folder and a graph per person, public facts only

concepts.title: ourselves first
concepts.what: The team's own pages first: they will say yes

concepts.title: the verified block
concepts.what: A dated note at the foot of a page of what several models checked

concepts.title: pack mode
concepts.what: sgit's efficient mode for large research vaults

concepts.title: deltas
concepts.what: Backups that store only what changed

concepts.title: agent power
concepts.what: The person's agent drafts; the person sends ("vicky.agent" format)

concepts.title: decisions as pages
concepts.what: A decision for Dinis made on a page with full details

concepts.title: the personal newsreel
concepts.what: A personalised debrief of the summit from everything published about it (from customers@'s brief, not these memos)

concepts.title: prompt on every page
concepts.what: A page's own llms.txt: a prompt to paste into one's own AI (from the events guidance, not these memos)
